content_voiceover: Cold agglutinin disease management starts with general measures for everyone, treat any secondary cause like infection, lymphoma, or autoimmune disease, avoid cold exposure by keeping the extremities warm, and always pre-warm blood products and IV fluids to prevent triggering hemolysis. Asymptomatic patients just need observation, supportive care, and folate. For symptomatic CAD, first line is rituximab, 375 milligrams per meter squared weekly for 4 weeks, with a response rate around 50 percent. Second line options push that response rate higher, rituximab combined with fludarabine or bendamustine gets response rates over 70 percent, and sutimlimab, a C1 inhibitor, was FDA approved in February 2022, giving rapid onset with a 54 percent response rate. For emergencies, you are looking at blood transfusion with an in-line warmer, plasma exchange, or the C5 inhibitor eculizumab. Unlike warm AIHA where steroids are first line, steroids are notably ineffective in CAD because it is an IgM mediated, complement driven process rather than an IgG mediated one. Also remember, consider LMWH prophylaxis in untreated patients with severe anemia or additional thrombotic risk factors.
keypoints: Sutimlimab (C1 inhibitor): rapid onset, RR 54%, FDA 2022
Steroids largely ineffective in CAD (unlike warm AIHA)
Always pre-warm blood products/fluids; avoid cold exposure
